Switching · Windows → macOS

Is there a Total Commander for Mac?

No — Total Commander is Windows-only. Christian Ghisler has never shipped a macOS build, and there is no official port planned. You have two routes: run the Windows version through a compatibility layer (Wine, CrossOver) or a Windows VM, or switch to a file manager built natively for the Mac.

The compatibility route keeps your muscle memory but gives up native Finder integration, retina rendering and Apple Silicon performance. The native route means learning a new tool, but every native Mac dual-pane manager below gives you the thing you actually came for: two directories side by side, keyboard-driven.

Questions people actually ask

Can I run Total Commander on a Mac with Wine or CrossOver?

Yes, and people do. Total Commander is a small, old-school Win32 application, which is the class of software Wine handles best. You give up native menu-bar integration, Finder tag and Quick Look support, and you take on a compatibility layer to maintain. A Windows VM (Parallels, VMware, UTM) is the more reliable version of the same trade — heavier, but it behaves like Windows because it is Windows.

Worth being clear about the trade: this route is right if you depend on specific Total Commander plugins. If you mainly want the two-panel workflow, a native tool will be faster and less fragile.

Which Mac file manager is closest to Total Commander?

Depends which part of Total Commander you mean:

  • The keyboard-first two-panel core → Marta or Nimble Commander. Both are native, both are free to start with.
  • The built-in FTP/SFTP and archive handling → ForkLift 4 or Nimble Commander. This is the part Total Commander users miss most.
  • The plugin ecosystem → nothing on macOS matches it. Marta has plugins, but it is a smaller ecosystem.

Double Commander and muCommander are also worth a look: both are free, open-source and cross-platform, which makes them the most literal ports of the idea — at the cost of not feeling especially Mac-native.

Do the F5 / F6 copy and move keys work on a Mac?

Not out of the box in Finder, and not identically anywhere. macOS reserves the function-key row for system features by default, so most Mac dual-pane managers use their own bindings rather than reproducing Total Commander's F-key layout literally. Nimble Commander is the closest to the classic Commander key map.

Diptychon uses a modifier chord instead of a function key: ⌥⌘→ sends the selection to the other panel, ⌥⌘← pulls it back. Different keys, same one-keystroke idea.

Is there a free Total Commander alternative for Mac?

Yes. Marta is free (though not open source), and Nimble Commander is free and open source, with a paid Pro tier for admin/root operations. Double Commander and muCommander are free and open source as well. None of them costs anything to try, so the honest advice is to try the free ones before paying for anything.

Where does Diptychon fit?

Diptychon is a native macOS dual-panel manager built keyboard-first: two panels, one chord to send files across, multi-level undo on move, copy, trash and rename, real Finder tags, and a 1.5 MB download. It is a one-time purchase rather than a subscription — the price is not set yet — and it collects no telemetry.

What it does not do matters for anyone coming from Total Commander, and the reasons differ — worth separating, because one of them is permanent and the others are not:

  • No FTP or SFTP. A deliberate boundary: v1 is local-only, and the app is built so it stays small. The internal seam that a remote source would plug into exists, but nothing is promised and nothing is scheduled.
  • No plugin runtime — gadgets instead. Not an omission, a different answer to the same need: a gadget hands the current selection to any app or CLI tool you name, with no plugin API to learn and nothing to install. Narrower than Total Commander's plugins, and it already ships.
  • No archive browsing. Not in v1. It is parked as a known gap rather than scheduled — it gets built if the people signing up ask for it, and dropped if they don't.

Diptychon is pre-1.0 and under active development, so this list is a snapshot, not a verdict. But do not pick a tool on a roadmap: if built-in FTP or a plugin ecosystem is why you use Total Commander today, ForkLift or Nimble Commander is the honest answer, and there is nothing to download here yet either way.

Come to Diptychon from Total Commander if…

  • You want the two-panel workflow, not the plugin ecosystem.
  • You work on local and mounted drives, not remote servers.
  • You want native and tiny, not Wine or a VM.
  • You want undo on file operations — Total Commander has none.

Stay where you are if…

  • You depend on Total Commander plugins.
  • You need FTP/SFTP inside the file manager.
  • You need it today — Diptychon has not launched.
  • You want archive browsing as folders.
